question: Can an appropriate assessment conducted after significant environmental degradation has already taken place satisfy the requirements of Article 6(3) of Directive 92/43/EEC (Habitats Directive), which requires prior assessment of plans or projects likely to have significant effects on protected sites?

Does the Commission consider that public participation requirements under the Aarhus Convention and Directive 2003/35/EC are fulfilled where local communities were not effectively consulted at the earliest stages of decision-making, particularly in cases involving retrospective applications?

Is the continued drainage and degradation of peatlands, pending decisions on retrospective consent, consistent with the EU’s climate objectives, including emissions reduction commitments and peatland restoration targets under relevant EU policies, and is the Commission aware of, and does it have concerns regarding, any potential systematic reliance by Ireland on retrospective planning mechanisms (such as substitute consent) in sectors including peat extraction, and their compatibility with EU environmental law?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.10.2026) Under Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive1 any appropriate assessment of a plan or project likely to have significant effects on a Natura 2000 site, must be carried out before the authorisation and implementation of that plan or project.

Public participation in environmental matters2 is an obligation on Member States authorities, to ensure that the public is consulted when all options are still open3. The Commission has been pursuing Ireland for many years for failures to control drainage and peat extraction. With regard to the Habitats Directive, the Commission brought infringement proceedings in Case C-196/254.

Regarding the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive5, Ireland removed the option for developers who started developments such as peat cutting without permission to apply to regularise these activities through retrospective retention permission in answer to the judgment in Case C-215/066. Ireland replaced this with a new substitute consent regime applicable only in exceptional cases.

The Commission is not aware that the substitute consent regime has been misused to retrospectively authorise peat extraction but there are continued concerns as regards alleged illegal peat extraction due to enforcement failures which resulted in the decision to further refer Ireland to court7 in 2026.

With regards to the greenhouse gas emissions related to drainage, the Commission has set national targets in the Land Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry sector. But Member States are free to choose how to achieve them according to their national circumstances. Nevertheless, peatland rewetting is one of the most effective measures in countries with a high proportion of drained organic soils.
